name: Asahel (son of Zeruiah)
title: One of David's mighty men and among the Thirty
summary: Asahel was the son of Zeruiah and brother to Joab and Abishai, and thus nephew of King David. He distinguished himself through his extraordinary speed, which was compared to a gazelle on the plain, and was counted among David's thirty mighty men. In addition, he served as commander of the fourth monthly division. After the battle at Gibeon, he pursued Abner, Saul's army commander, but was killed when Abner struck him with the back end of his spear. Asahel's death triggered a bloody feud between Joab and Abner that would characterize David's early kingdom. The episode illustrates the tension between personal honor and clan-based blood vengeance on one side, and the need for political stability in the young Israelite kingdom on the other.

keyEvents.title: One of David's thirty mighty men
keyEvents.description: Asahel was counted among David's thirty brave warriors who distinguished themselves in battle and were known for their loyalty to David.

keyEvents.title: Swift as a gazelle
keyEvents.description: Asahel was famous for his speed and was compared to a gazelle in the field, which made him a fearsome warrior on the battlefield.

keyEvents.title: The Pursuit of Abner
keyEvents.description: After the battle at Gibeon, Asahel pursued Abner without turning to the right or left, determined to catch up with him.

keyEvents.title: Killed by Abner
keyEvents.description: Despite Abner's repeated warnings to give up the pursuit, Asahel continued. Abner struck him with the back end of his spear so that it went through his body, and Asahel died on the spot.

keyEvents.title: Burial in Bethlehem
keyEvents.description: Asahel was buried in his father's tomb in Bethlehem. His death caused deep grief and became a turning point that triggered a bloody cycle of revenge.

keyEvents.title: Joab's Revenge for Asahel's Death
keyEvents.description: Asahel's death was later avenged when his brother Joab tricked Abner aside at the gate of Hebron and killed him. This created major political problems for King David, who publicly condemned the murder.

keyEvents.title: Leader of the Fourth Military Division
keyEvents.description: Asahel is mentioned as the leader of the fourth monthly military division, a position that after his death was taken over by his son Shebaja.

versions.summary: Asahel was one of David's three nephews, the son of Zeruiah and brother to Joab and Abishai. He was known for his extraordinary speed and was one of David's thirty mighty men. His death at Abner's hand triggered a bloody feud that characterized David's early reign.
versions.title: David's Swift Warriors
versions.reason: [minor] Asahel is not described as a 'commander' in the Bible. He was one of David's thirty mighty men and known as a warrior, but there is no clear biblical source that gives him the role of commander. In 1 Chronicles 27:7 he is mentioned as leader of one of the army divisions, but it is his son Zebadiah who took over after him. The role can be retained with some justification, but 'one of David's thirty mighty men' is more precise.; [minor] Asahel's father is unknown in the Bible – Zeruiah was his mother, and the identity of his father is never explicitly mentioned. That the father is null is therefore correct. Some traditions identify the father as a man named Nahash, but this is uncertain.; [minor] The text says 'his father's grave in Bethlehem', but the Bible states that he was buried in his father's grave. Since the identity of the father is unknown but the grave is mentioned, the wording is acceptable. However, it is worth noting that this is one of the few places where the father is indirectly mentioned.; [minor] A reference from 1 Chronicles 2:16 could be added to confirm the family relationships (that Zeruiah was the mother of Abishai, Joab and Asahel), as well as 1 Chronicles 11:26 and 27:7 which give further information about Asahel.; [minor] The role 'one of David's thirty mighty men' could have been included as an explicit role to provide a more complete picture.; [major] Footnotes are missing. A profile should have at least some footnotes covering linguistic, historical or theological details – for example about the name Asahel, the gazelle comparison, or Zeruiah's unique role as matriarch in the genealogies.

"David's swift warriors and one of the thirty mighty men" is descriptive and accurate.; [minor] The field 'father' is set to null, which is acceptable since the Bible does not directly name Serujah's husband. Some traditions link Nahash or another person to Serujah, but this is uncertain. Null is an acceptable value here.; [minor] The summary is well-written and informative. A small improvement could be made by clarifying that his role as a military commander was also significant.; [minor] The footnote about Serujah is categorized as 'theological', but its content deals more with genealogy and socio-historical practice. footnotes.text: The name Asahel (Hebrew: עֲשָׂהאֵל, 'Asa'el') means 'God has made/created'. It is a theophoric name that testifies to the parents' faith in God's creative work.

The comparison with a gazelle (Hebrew: צְבִי, tsevi) in 2 Sam 2:18 uses an image well known in the ancient Near East. The gazelle symbolized speed and agility, and similar comparisons are also found in the description of Gad's warriors in 1 Chr 12:8.

Serah is unusual in biblical material because she—not a father—is used as a family identifier for her sons. This may indicate that she was the most well-known of the parents, possibly due to kinship with David's family. According to 1 Chr 2:16, Serah was David's sister.

Gibeon, where the decisive battle took place (2 Sam 2:12–17), is identified with modern el-Jib, northwest of Jerusalem. Archaeological excavations have revealed a large water reservoir that may correspond to 'the pool at Gibeon' mentioned in the text.

The fact that Abner killed Asahel with the back end of his spear (2 Sam 2:23) is an unusual detail that underscores that Abner did not want to kill him. In ancient warfare, one would normally use the spearhead. This shows Abner's reluctance and makes Joab's later act of revenge even more morally questionable.

Asahel's name appears in the list of leaders for the military divisions in 1 Chr 27:7, where it states that his son Shebuel took over after him. This may indicate that the position was hereditary, or that Shebuel was appointed as an honor to his father's memory.

Blood vengeance was an established practice in ancient Israel and the Near East. Joab's revenge killing of Abner for the murder of Asahel can be understood within the framework of this custom, even though David clearly distanced himself from the act (2 Sam 3:28–29). This episode illustrates the tension between clan-based justice and royal authority in the young Israelite monarchy.
